lastCommit.message:
OTA-1850 — a Resurrection Gem belongs to the Tartarian who earned it

THE PRODUCT RULING. Gems were install-wide, which let a player farm them on
characters they did not care about and spend them on the one they did. They are
now character-bound: earned BY someone, spendable only BY them. Deleting a
character does not release their gems, switching characters switches the
balance, and there is no pool, no transfer and no gifting. Reward amounts, the
one-gem cost, drop rates, boss eligibility and vendor behaviour are all
unchanged — this moves ownership, not economy.

THE DURABILITY REPAIR, WHICH IS THE SAME CHANGE. Three reproduced crash bugs
shared one shape: two durable stores, one commit ordering, no idempotency
marker. The balance lived in the global stash while the thing it paid for — the
revival, the "already paid" keepsake mark — lived in the character's own slot
key, and AsyncStorage has no cross-key transaction. Moving the balance onto the
character deletes the second store, so:

  · the gem spend and the revival are one write to one record. Neither
    "charged and still dead" nor "alive and never charged" is a state the
    storage can hold, so NO boot reconciliation machinery is added — there is
    nothing left to reconcile.
  · the boss keepsake's gem and its onceLootPaid mark land in the same store
    update and the same persist(). Hazard C closes by shape.
  · the dev-name death grant rides inside the death write instead of racing
    the persist() of the very record it was crediting.

What still needs a mechanism is concurrency on ONE record, and that is
mutateSlot — deliberately the same shape as OTA-1835's mutateGlobalStash: one
serialized queue per slot, load → mutate → save, sentinel for no-write.

A DEATH NOW HAS ITS OWN IDENTITY. newDeathId() is minted at the death site and
persisted with the character, so a resurrection retry after a crash is free
while a LATER death costs again. The previously proposed
`slotId|characterSeed|floor(hoursElapsed)` was dropped on evidence: two genuine
deaths inside one floored game hour collide, which would have made the second
resurrection free.

THE LEGACY HANDOVER, AND WHAT IT HONESTLY IS. The old shared pool is divided
once across surviving characters in proportion to their DURABLE IN-WORLD GAME
HOURS (hoursElapsed), by largest remainder, with a stable lexical slotId
tie-break and exact conservation. This is a best-effort HEURISTIC, not
provenance — nothing in the old data records who earned a gem — and two
better-sounding rules were rejected on evidence: Fallen death counts are
unattributable (FallenHero carries no character identity and the list is capped
at 25) and savedAt−createdAt measures wall-clock elapsed, not play. It is game
time, not wall-clock playtime, and a brand-new character reads zero.

The plan is computed ONCE and then obeyed: the input snapshot is persisted
beside the result (original total, total hours, per-slot hours and allocation,
and whether the weighted rule or the active-character fallback applied), so a
restart replays the same rows rather than recomputing against hours that have
since moved. More play, a different active character, or a reordered index all
read the same answer. The handover runs at boot, before the roster is drawn, so
each record's own count is true on screen. With no characters yet the pool is
HELD rather than split — that is the fresh-install seed, one free gem per
install, claimed by the first character created.

THE COUNT MOVED TO THE DOSSIER. The title screen's global gem chit is gone and
nothing replaces it: there is no install-wide figure left for it to show. The
number reads on the character's own record, in the dossier's existing meta
voice, and the resurrect/fallen decision and its confirm copy ask that
character's balance rather than a shared total.

Tests: new permanent suite ota1850GemsBelongToTheCharacter (50) covering the
farming case, one-write spend/revive, retry-vs-later-death, per-record
concurrency, the allocation arithmetic, the one-time handover, the install seed
and the retired install-wide paths. Four neighbouring suites were re-pointed at
the new architecture with their claims strengthened, not weakened: OTA-1394 now
requires that no spend ordering can exist rather than that a particular order is
chosen; OTA-1830 §5.5 requires the keepsake gem and its paid-mark to share one
synchronous update instead of requiring a .then to sit on; OTA-1833 §2.1 follows
the gem authority to gemsAfterGrant; OTA-1835's stash-field list grows by
legacyGemMigration on the same reasoning OTA-1844 and OTA-1845 used.

Six negative controls, each restored byte-identical. One of them (NC-C, first
attempt) did NOT bite and that was a fault in the control rather than the code:
dropping the LAST leftover is a no-op because the remainder is always strictly
smaller than the row count. Re-run as a genuine off-by-one it turned E1 and E3
red.
